evidences.evidence_context:
It is worth noting that the aforementioned eavesdropping attacks are considered invasive attacks, requiring the eavesdropper to either physically tamper with the victim's device or install malware on it. On the other hand, some eavesdropping methods [10], [12], [13], [24], [25] rely on pre-established vocabulary of hot words and are limited to tasks such as word classification, speaker identification, or gender identification. In contrast to these methods, our proposed approach belongs to a non-intrusive attack and does not rely on pre-established vocabulary. This significantly enhances its practicality in real-world scenarios.
Non-intrusive eavesdropping attacks are continually being developed. For instance, [8], [9] employ WiFi Received Signal Strength (RSS) and Channel State Information (CSI) analysis, respectively, to identify specific words. Another approach [31], based on Impulse Radio Ultra-Wideband, recovers and separates sound from multiple sources. However, these methods face challenges such as limited vibration resolution due to longer wavelengths and the need for large antenna setups, which increases operational difficulty in real-world scenarios. Moreover, mmWave-based eavesdropping attacks have been explored. For instance, mmEve [4] captures mmWave signals emitted by smartphones in earphone mode to recover speech. Wavesdropper [32] uses millimeter waves to eavesdrop on human speech in through-wall scenarios. Another method proposed in [5] employs piezoelectric film and millimeter wave signals for voice eavesdropping. mmSpy [6] also utilizes mmWave for eavesdropping on phone conversations but treats it as a classification problem, limiting its ability to recognize specific keywords or numbers. Additionally, [7] can reconstruct high-quality sound from the user's throat using millimeter-wave radar, but it requires the subject to remain motionless and maintain a short distance from the radar probe.
Optical eavesdropping is the most relevant eavesdropping technique to this article. The visual microphone [33] captures subtle surface vibrations of objects using a high-speed camera (2200 FPS). However, this method demands significant computing resources and high hardware requirements, resulting in several hours of processing time to recover a few seconds of audio. Laser microphones [20], [21], [22], [23], [34] use lidar sensors to illuminate vibrating objects and collect reflected signals for audio reconstruction.
